item.title: US approves Iraqi government integrating Iran-backed factions in new cabinet
item.description:
US approves Iraqi government integrating Iran-backed factions in new cabinet

Washington has approved the inclusion of Iran-backed factions in the new Iraqi government, according to diplomatic sources.

A source told AFP that Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi "obtained the tacit approval of the United States" during his visit in September for the United Nations General Assembly, where he met with President Donald Trump.

The main point of contention was the appointment of Laith al-Khazali, brother of Qais al-Khazali - leader of the US-designated group Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq - to a position in the cabinet.

The approval came "after the Prime Minister promised to move forward with his disarmament plans and provided guarantees that these groups would not attack American interests in Iraq."

item.title: 'Truly desperate' humanitarian crisis in Yemen will get worse, warns WFP
item.description:
'Truly desperate' humanitarian crisis in Yemen will get worse, warns WFP

The "truly desperate" humanitarian crisis in Yemen is only going to get worse as a result of the renewed conflict, the World Food Programme has warned.

“Yemen was already one of the top concerns as hunger hot spots in the world, which means that people in Yemen were already hungry, they were reliant on imported food or humanitarian assistance,” said Samantha Chattaraj, World Food Programme deputy country director for Yemen, speaking to Al-Jazeera.

“Now that we have lost access to over 800,000 people who were reliant on our assistance until last month, the situation is going to get even more catastrophic."

“I think we are at a very critical juncture. If we do not restore the right operating environment and facilitate access to bring back assistance to them, we are going from hunger to starvation."

item.title: Iran's Hatami says Hormuz under 'full supervision' of army, IRGC
item.description:
Iran's Hatami says Hormuz under 'full supervision' of army, IRGC

Iran’s Army Commander-in-Chief Amir Hatami has said that the Strait of Hormuz is under the "full supervision" of the army and the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps, Iran’s Mehr news agency reported.

“The Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the enemy respects the rights of the Iranian people,” he said.

Hatami claimed that “not a single enemy vessel has dared to enter the Sea of Oman to this day, except for three vessels that came and were fired upon by us"

“We took decisive action, and today they know that traffic is very, very limited.”

item.title: Morning update
item.description:
Morning update

Good Morning Middle East Eye readers,

If you are just joining us, here are key developments from across the region and beyond:

* US President Donald Trump has said he is weighing fresh strikes on Iran without nuclear weapons or ground troops, while insisting negotiations with Tehran were under way.

* Saudi Arabia's Deputy Foreign Minister Waleed Elkhereiji has said Houthi attacks on civilian, economic and airport facilities in the kingdom “constitute full-fledged war crimes”.

* At least five people were killed in Houthi missile strikes near the al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden on Thursday. The prime minister and other officials were safe but two of his bodyguards were killed.

* Yemen's Ansar Allah (Houthis) has claimed responsibility for the attack on the government headquarters in Aden, with its armed forces spokesperson, Yahya Saree, describing the building as housing "Saudi war operations room".

* The UN Security Council has condemned the "escalatory" attacks by Yemen's Houthis on Saudi Arabia, including "reckless strikes" on Riyadh's airport.

* Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Israeli President Isaac Herzog that Israel should stop and reverse its "forced establishment" of West Bank settlements, China's foreign ministry said in a statement on Friday.

* Israeli settlers torched vehicles owned by Palestinians during an attack on olive harvesters on Friday morning near the town of Turmus Ayya, north of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Quds News Network reported. 

* An Israeli settlement group has said that it has established a new settlement facing Gaza City, and urged the Israeli government to immediately authorise its transfer into the northern part of the Strip.

* Several displaced Gazans were injuries on Thursday evening following an Israeli strike west of Gaza City, Wafa reported.

* Saudi Arabia has said preparations for the 2027 AFC Asian Cup, due to begin on 7 January in Riyadh, Jeddah and Al Khobar, remain on schedule despite escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom.

* Iraq’s parliament has approved Laith al-Khazali, a senior figure from the Iran-backed Asaib Ahl al-Haq movement, as a deputy prime minister.

* Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree has said the group shot down a Saudi Wing Loong II armed reconnaissance drone over Marib governorate.

* A drone launched towards Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province was intercepted and destroyed, Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said.  

* The Trump administration has issued fresh Iran-related sanctions targeting 16 individuals and 10 entities, according to a notice posted on the US Treasury Department’s website on Thursday, Reuters reported.

* Two air strikes have targeted Houthi positions in the Dhi al-Barih and Jaba areas of al-Misrakh district, south of Taiz city, Al Jazeera reported, citing a Yemeni military source in the Taiz military command.

 * The threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remains "severe", the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre says, warning further attacks in the waterway were "highly likely" under current conditions.

item.title: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
item.description:
Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.

The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz, the country’s former prime minster has said.

Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed, now an adviser to Yemen’s president, said it would be catastrophic if the city fell to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, since control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea and the road to Aden – the site of the UN-recognised government – would be lost.

The US government could spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on a media campaign in South Africa to figure out why more white Afrikaners are not applying to become refugees to the US, as Donald Trump had hoped.

State department officials, according to an August proposal seen by the Guardian, outlined a roughly $335,000 research and advertising effort after applications to the refugee program “trended lower than expected” since Afrikaners were allowed to apply directly online in November 2025. The document, written by the US mission in South Africa with a department research unit for the embassy in Pretoria, admits officials know little about why.
